Prevention: This disease is caused by a phytoplasma which lives within the phloem of the stem; use only disease-free plants in the field as planting material
Restrict the movement of planting materials from infested areas to avoid spreading the disease
Do not plant new plots of cassava next to those that have the disease
Control weeds near the field which may act as alternate hosts and thus reservoirs for the disease
Monitoring: Plants: stunting and excessive proliferation of branches from a single point
Shoots: small leaves and shortened internodes, without distortion or chlorosis
Proliferation of a few stunted weak shoots from the cuttings
Stems: brown vascular tissues when cut.
Leaves: small, curling and yellow/green patterns
Root: thin and woody with thick outer layers and deep cracks which sometimes form a ring around it
Not all of these symptoms may be present
Act as soon as symptoms of the disease are seen in the field
Symtoms of small, deformed leaves in bunches can look similar to those caused by the cassava mealybug ( Phenacoccus manihoti ).
The mealybugs are a few millimetres long, oval, rose-pink and dusted with white powdery wax.
They leave whitish, woolly egg sacks on the plant and may be accompanied by ants
Direct Control: Elimination of infected plants by burning or burying
Control insects in the field that might be transmitting the disease.
Plant and leaf hoppers are the most likely vectors, however the transmission route is still under investigation and the exact vector is as yet unknown
